label: conflict meetings and facilitation
overview: Conflict meeting scenarios require the advisor to act as a facilitator — not an adjudicator. The goal is never to declare a winner. It is to create an environment where people can catch themselves acting in violation of their own higher values, and choose to let go of their current position for the greater good. The psychological foundation is understanding why people double down on positions even when proven wrong — and building a safe cognitive pathway for them to release those positions without feeling a loss of self. The practical tools are the 6-step facilitation process, the Force Field Analysis whiteboard exercise, the 3 framing concepts, and deliberate status management.

diagnostic_entry.primary_question: Is the conflict between two parties who share the same ultimate goal but disagree on the process — or are their interests genuinely opposed, making a mutually acceptable outcome structurally difficult?
diagnostic_entry.shared_goal_different_process: This is the most resolvable form of conflict. Find the early alignment on the shared outcome quickly, then separate the outcome from the process. Redirect energy from what went wrong to how to get where everyone wants to go.
diagnostic_entry.genuinely_opposed_interests: Use the Cliff Face and Grab Rails technique — show both parties the extreme consequence of scorched earth tactics, then offer a central equitable outcome they can agree to live with. The key is equitable, not equal. Equal means everyone gets the same; equitable means everyone gets what they need relative to their situation.
diagnostic_entry.entrenched_position_with_loss_of_self: The conflict has become about identity, not just interests. Before any process can work, the facilitator must open the cognitive pathway for detachment using the Santa Claus sequence. Attempting to resolve the substantive issue before addressing the loss-of-self dynamic will fail — the party cannot hear the solution until they feel safe enough to let go.

materials.name: Conflict Psychology — Detachment and the Cognitive Pathway
materials.summary: Explains why people dig in. Because we process new information by association with past experience, we take personal ownership of our understanding — so conflicting evidence does not feel like information, it feels like a loss of self or a moment of embarrassment. That is why people double down on a position they can see is wrong. The facilitator's job is to build a cognitive pathway that lets someone separate their emotional attachment from the belief itself.
materials.who_when: Advisors preparing to facilitate any meeting where positions are already entrenched — before the room is booked, not once the argument has started.
steps: Expect the double-down and read it correctly: it is the fear of learning we are wrong, not stubbornness or bad faith.
Name the real cost to the person — letting go of a stated belief risks a feeling of loss of self, or short-term embarrassment in front of people whose opinion they value.
Build the cognitive pathway before challenging anything, so the client can detach their emotional attachment from the belief and examine it as a separate object.
Choose a tool that lets people describe the situation from a distance — as if observing an external group — rather than one that asks them to defend their own ego in the room.
Map the instinctual drives of self-preservation at work: avoiding pain versus gaining pleasure.
Use that read to decide whether the group needs to tune in to the proposed change or tune out of the position they are defending.

materials.name: Force Field Analysis — The 6-Step Conflict Meeting
materials.summary: The whiteboard exercise built for groups with real potential for conflict, run as a six-step meeting. It works because participants describe the situation at arm's length instead of defending themselves directly, and because the worst-case picture is drawn deliberately early to create the desire to act. Its governing rule is play the ball, not the player.
materials.who_when: Facilitated group sessions where the parties disagree and the meeting could go badly — partnerships, families in dispute, management teams stuck on a decision.
steps: Establish status and frame the session — call out the ghosts by naming poor behaviour or underlying fears in advance, and co-opt a vocal adversary by giving them a real task, such as making the clock-watcher the official timekeeper.
Deliver it congruently — matched gesture and pace, genuine intent for a positive outcome, and clear conceptual frameworks that show the session was thought about beforehand.

Define the rules and find early alignment — state what behaving badly looks like, have each participant make a promise and ask permission, and set realistic expectations for a fair solution so nobody is rewarded for opening with an extreme demand.
Separate outcome from method — find the people who want the same end result but disagree on how, and make that distinction explicit early.
Open the analysis with WHY (the purpose of the model), WHAT (the action plan) and HOW (play the ball, not the player).
Draw the Perfect World position first — where the group would ideally be — to shift the frame to what is possible and open minds.
Draw the Worst Case position next, deliberately. Describing a dire situation at a distance lessens guilt, and the fear of that outcome is what generates the desire to act — let it linger.

List the pushing forces (the benefits of change) and the holding forces (constraints such as lack of funds, or fear). Run this as a productive bloodletting, and stop personal attacks the moment they appear.
When positions harden, show the Cliff Face — the mutually assured consequences of scorched-earth tactics — and offer the Grab Rails, a central outcome everyone can live with.
Use time and space when energy peaks: call a short coffee break and send everyone away to return with one constructive suggestion that does not come at someone else's cost.
Drive the action plan out of the whiteboard — concrete tasks with automated reminders, copying in the relevant people so visibility carries it to completion.

advisor_guidance.facilitator_not_adjudicator: The moment the advisor takes a position on the substantive content of the conflict, they lose their authority as a neutral facilitator. The role is to manage the process — not to determine who is right. If the advisor has a prior relationship with one party, that relationship must be explicitly acknowledged and set aside at the opening of the meeting.
advisor_guidance.cliff_face_without_grab_rails_is_dangero: The Cliff Face technique is powerful precisely because it uses fear. But fear without a safe exit triggers panic, escalation, or walkouts — not resolution. Every time the Cliff Face is shown, the Grab Rails must immediately follow. Show the consequence; then show the path. Never one without the other.
advisor_guidance.equitable_not_equal: Most persistent conflict is sustained by both parties arguing for equality when the situation actually demands equity. The facilitator must hold this distinction clearly and introduce it early — before positions become entrenched around the wrong standard. Once parties understand that equitable means each person gets what their situation requires, rather than identical shares, resolution becomes structurally possible.
advisor_guidance.use_breaks_deliberately: Private reflection is both the greatest risk (buyers remorse and backtracking) and the greatest opportunity (genuine processing away from group pressure) in a conflict meeting. Never call a break without assigning a specific reflection task. The task redirects the private thinking from relitigating the conflict to generating progress.
advisor_guidance.loss_of_self_must_be_addressed_first: Advisors who attempt to resolve the substantive issue before addressing the loss-of-self dynamic will fail — often repeatedly. The party cannot hear the solution while they are gripping their identity. The Santa Claus sequence and the prescribed cognitive pathway are not optional warm-ups; they are the structural prerequisite for everything that follows.
